6.text: Dogs of the southern and western districts are considered the swiftest and

7.text: the most enduring. Among the Russianized natives the large and shaggy

8.text: dogs of the Indighirka River are especially valued; among the Kamchadal,

9.text: those of the southwestern villages Yavina and Golyghina; and among the

10.text: Koryak, those of the Poqaˊč. The Chukchee dogs are considered the poorest
10.resolved: Poqaˊč = P+o+q+a, stress U+02CA, č = c+U+030C

11.text: of all, probably on account of their more scanty diet. Therefore the trade in

12.text: live dogs between the Russian settlements in Anadyr and the Chukchee villages

13.text: on the Pacific shore is of importance. A good dog can be bought with four

14.text: or five white fox-skins, or two dogs with an American shotgun with accessories, etc.

15.text: Kamchadal, Koryak, and Russian dogs are fed exclusively on fish, — raw,

16.text: dried, or frozen, according to the season or the locality (Plate VI, Fig. 3).
16.note: Printed roman numeral "vi" is set genuinely lowercase (x-height, not small-cap or full-cap height); keyed ASCII capital VI per keying_spec.md §2.12, "Every roman numeral in the book is keyed in plain ASCII capitals, whatever the setting."

17.text: The Kolyma Russians often cook for their dogs a kind of porridge made of

18.text: putrid fish, roe, fish-bones, refuse of human food, etc., and serve it in long

19.text: wooden trays; but this kind of food is convenient only at times of rest, since

20.text: the dogs feel heavy with too much liquid food. The Chukchee dogs are fed

21.text: on the intestines of seals, and on seal, walrus, and whale blubber. Their share

22.text: of meat is small, and consists only of kitchen refuse, since their masters want

23.text: all the meat proper for themselves. However, exclusive blubber diet is insuf-

24.text: ficient for dogs. In the summer-time, in the Chukchee villages of the Pacific

25.text: coast, I saw large pieces of blubber strewn all over the ground; and the dogs
25.note: small ink speck between "the" and "ground", above the baseline gutter; not a letterform or mark, ruled a print speck and not keyed.

26.text: prowling among them did not appear to be overfed. The natives said, that,

27.text: whenever the dogs were satiated, they would desist from eating blubber for

28.text: a long time. On the contrary, in the fishing villages of the Koryak or Kam-

29.text: chadal, at the same season, when food is scattered on the ground, the dogs

30.text: grow so fat that they can hardly walk.¹
30.note: footnote reference marker; mz draft dropped it entirely ("walk." with no digit). Raster shows a clear raised 1 after the period, paired with the opener on line 43.

31.text: The continuous fluctuations of success in seal-hunting, and the frequent

32.text: seasons of famine, have a deteriorating effect upon the Chukchee race of dogs;

33.text: but fishing among the more southern tribes is much more regular. Chukchee

34.text: dogs need something to season their blubber, and are generally inclined to

35.text: eat up all the dry thongs they can get; they even gnaw at the lashings of

36.text: sledges, and destroy their own harness and traces, much more than do the

37.text: southern fish-fed dogs. On the contrary, the Russian fish-fed dogs thrive best

38.text: when they are given blubber mixed with their dried fish. The dogs are fed

39.text: once a day, usually in the evening, by some of the drivers immediately after

40.text: stopping; while others prefer to wait until they have had three hours of rest.

41.text: A piece of blubber measuring two inches each way, and some shreds of putrid

42.text: walrus-meat or whale-skin, form the daily ration of every dog. During the
